changes.summary: Roger's links in the group chat work again. When he ended a sentence with a link — "Review your plan at theleague.us/rosters." — GroupMe grabbed the period along with the address and sent everyone who tapped it to a page that doesn't exist. The roster-cutdown reminder is the one owners actually noticed, since it's the message telling seven teams to go log in and fix their roster. Two fixes, because one wasn't enough: every bot message now gets the trailing period trimmed off the link on the way out, and the site itself now catches a link that arrives with a period stuck to it and quietly sends you to the right page instead of a dead end. That second half matters, because the messages already sitting in the chat can't be edited — and it works for links you paste into a text message or an email too.

Computer Jocks and Da Dangsters now look the same at night in both leagues. Both teams play in TheLeague and the AFL with the identical crest, and both were getting a different dark-mode treatment on each side. Computer Jocks had a dark file over here that was just the normal logo with a white line painted around it — which is exactly what the site already does on its own, so the file's gone and the outline is now drawn in the team's green, same as the AFL. Da Dangsters keeps its dark version, but it's the newer artwork the AFL got last week: the crest on its own navy backdrop instead of the old white-ringed one. Same logo, one look, whichever league you're reading.

Balls Deep gets a dark-mode crest of its own. The witch was always readable enough at night to skip the thin white outline the site traces around the darker logos, so this one didn't have to change — it did anyway. The crest now sits on its own near-black backdrop with the outline drawn in by hand rather than added by the site, which keeps the hat and the black dress from bleeding into the card behind them. Same witch, better edges.

Four more AFL crests traded the white dark-mode outline for a color of their own. The thin ring that keeps a dark logo readable on a dark card is white by default, which is fine for a default and a little rude to a team that owns a color — Midwestside's gold ring has looked right since the day it shipped, where a white one around a gold-and-black crest read like packaging. Computer Jocks now get their green, The Show the dusty pink off its label, and No Soup For You that orange-red. Jewpacabra is the odd one out: the pixel check had said its crest didn't need a ring at all, because it counts how much of a logo is bright and Jewpacabra is bright right through the middle. What it doesn't count is the rim, which is dark, which is why that crest's edge quietly dissolved into the card. It gets a green ring now. The measurement is a filter, not a verdict — and that goes both ways.

A Bruin Pegs Me dropped the dark-mode outline. The thin white ring gets traced around any crest a pixel-by-pixel check says is too dark to read on a dark card, and the bruin scored low enough to qualify — but the logo has enough bright detail inside it to hold its own, and the ring just read as a sticker edge somebody put around it. The measurement is a filter, not a verdict; this one got overruled. Every other crest that needs the outline still wears it.

Fullybaked, the Avenging Amish and Da Dangsters get their dark-mode logos. All three crests were drawn on a white puck, which looked fine all day and then sat on your dark screen at night like somebody left the lights on in one window. Same artwork, navy backdrop, swapped automatically the moment the site goes dark — so the icons now blend into the card instead of punching a hole in it. Vitside Mafia got this treatment a while back. Da Dangsters had been getting by on the thin white outline, and drops it here — which is exactly what that outline was always meant to do the moment real dark artwork showed up for a team. Everyone else who needs it is still wearing theirs.

Every AFL team logo on the site was being fetched from a second address instead of the page you were already on. It worked, but it meant your phone had to go open a whole separate connection just to draw a handful of 100-pixel crests — and on a cell signal they'd still be arriving well after everything else had finished. Nobody would have called it a bug; it just felt like the logos were slow. They're now served from the same place as the rest of the page, which also means they can't go missing if that other address ever moves. Roughly a dozen of them on the homepage, two dozen on the standings page.

The standings cards on both homepages swapped team names for team logos. On a phone the team column was eating half the row to spell out names you already know by their crest, which squeezed the numbers you actually came for. Now it's the logo, and the records and points get room to breathe. Dark mode got the harder half of this problem: a good chunk of the league wears a black or near-black logo, and once the crest is the only thing naming the row, a black logo on a black card names nothing. Every crest was measured against the dark card, and the ones that failed now get a thin white outline traced around the logo itself — so Badd Boys and Da Dangsters and the rest stay readable at night without anybody having to redraw them. Teams that already have a proper dark-mode logo still just switch to it. Screen readers still read the team name, and if a logo ever fails to load the name comes back in its place.

The Pecking Order's award cards stopped color-coding by team and started color-coding by meaning. Heater of the Week now runs a hot orange-red edge, Cooler of the Week an ice blue one, and the Bench Blunder gets pink — so the three you actually scan for are findable without reading the labels. Every other award still wears the winning franchise's color, and all of them are picked to stay legible in dark mode.

Every link Roger and Schefter drop in the group chat said the league's name twice. theleague.us/theleague/calendar. afl-fantasy.com/afl-fantasy/news. They worked — a redirect quietly cleaned it up on the way through — but you were reading the ugly version, and every tap paid for a round trip it didn't need. The folder name only exists so both leagues can share one site; on your own league's domain it's noise. Roger's countdowns, Schefter's Trade Builder invites, the Cut Watch and Gauntlet links, and the cutdown-deadline nags now all point straight at the clean address. The links also got pinned to the same address you actually browse, so they should stop occasionally opening you logged out.

Reporting a wrong answer now actually reaches the Commissioner. When the report button shipped, hitting it wrote the report to the database and put a red banner on the card — which is useful if somebody happens to be looking at that card, and useless otherwise. Reports now ride the same weekly channel as Roger's own self-audit: a reported answer gets posted to the group chat the week it's flagged and opens a tracked item that keeps nagging until it's dealt with. There's also finally a way to mark one handled, which clears the banner for everyone once the rulebook and the answer agree again.

Roger now tells you when he thinks he blew a call. His weekly self-audit had already caught the taxi squad blunder on July 27th — two days after the question was asked — and written a perfectly accurate diagnosis of it into a file in the repo, where it sat for seventeen days until the wrong answer got noticed in the group chat instead. The detection was never the problem. The delivery was: the job did its homework and went back to sleep. Now a flagged answer posts to the group chat the week it's found, so you know not to lean on it before Brandon rules. Repeat nagging stays on the commissioner's to-do list rather than your phone, and a quiet week posts nothing at all.

At 1:00 in the morning, Roger woke up the AFL to announce the draft was one week away. Two things wrong with that sentence. The draft is not one week away — the AL board goes live Saturday August 29 and the NL email draft opens the next morning, which is sixteen days out, and which is what the calendar has said the whole time. Roger was reading off a hardcoded August 20 that traces back to an old "annual draft window" line and matches nothing the league actually does. He now reads the same Labor Day math the calendar does, so there is exactly one draft date in the building. And the 1am part: every other thing Schefter sends respects overnight quiet hours. Roger's reminders somehow never got the memo, so whenever a countdown came due — 1am, 3am, whenever the scanner happened to tick — your phone found out. He now holds until 7am like everyone else. The two bogus countdown posts have been pulled from the feed. The GroupMe messages, unfortunately, are forever. While we were in there: the rulebook itself was the original source of the bad date. "Annual draft window: August 20 – August 25" has been sitting in the constitution, the rules page, and Roger's reference copy for years, describing a window the league has never actually drafted in. Per the Commissioner, the draft is always the weekend BEFORE Labor Day weekend — AL on the Saturday, NL on the Sunday morning after. All three now say that, in those words, so nothing downstream has to guess a date again. And one more, caught while reviewing the fix: Roger had the trade deadline wrong too, by exactly a week. He was set to start the countdown for November 11th. The deadline is November 18th — the Wednesday between Weeks 10 and 11, which is what the calendar has always shown. Same root cause, same fix.

The pinned League Office card explaining the 5th-year team option had the price wrong, and had it wrong since March. It said the option salary is the top 5 positional average. It's the top 10 — which is what the constitution has always said, what the rules page has always said, and what the site's own salary math has always calculated. Only the explainer was off. The likely culprit is that the Rookie Extension formula genuinely does use the top 5 positional average, the two rules sit next to each other, and they're mutually exclusive on the same player, so it's a very easy wire to cross. Different numbers, on purpose. If you did any 2026 first-rounder planning off that card, the option is pricier than you were told.

Roger blew a call, and the constitution is why. Gridiron Geeks asked whether taxi squad players count toward the 20-player-under-contract minimum, and Roger said no — reasoning, quite confidently, that the taxi squad is a separate animal from the 22-man active roster. It is separate. That was never the question. The rule says 20 players UNDER CONTRACT, and a taxi squad rookie is under contract, which is exactly why he's eating half his base salary against your cap. Same for anyone parked on IR. The Commissioner has ruled: if he's signed to your franchise, he counts, wherever he's sitting. The rulebook now says so in plain English instead of leaving a chatbot to infer it, and Roger's test suite has a case for this one so he can't talk himself back into it.

And then there was one. 2004 was the last season we couldn't rebuild — six divisions feeding an eight-team bracket meant the playoff field wasn't simply the top four in each conference, and without knowing who actually qualified there were three different ways to read that season's games. The fix came from an unexpected direction: the NIT. Sixteen teams played in it, the league has twenty-four, and nobody plays in both — so identifying the NIT field identified the championship field by subtraction. The AFL Losers Bracket then accounted for six of those eight, leaving exactly two teams standing, and MFL's own records name the winner: Bukkake Warriors 133.6, Your Team Sucks 106.44. Every game of 2004 is now on the page, from that title game down to the wonderfully named "2nd and 3rd Round NIT Losers." That's twenty seasons rebuilt. The only one left blank is 2003, which was played on Yahoo and never existed in MFL at all.

2011 finally has a playoff bracket, and it took some doing. Every other season we rebuilt by assuming the playoff field was the top four in each conference — which is how the AFL seeds it, except in 2011, when six divisions fed an eight-team bracket and two teams from outside the top eight got in on division titles. Feed the wrong eight teams into a bracket and it falls apart immediately, which is exactly what happened. So instead of guessing the qualification rule, the site now works backward from the shape: find the four week-14 games whose winners play each other in week 15, whose winners meet in week 16. Only one arrangement of that season's games fits, and it turned out to be Delirium Tremens over Drunk Indians 154.94 to 147.95. All ten of 2011's brackets are now on the page, from the title game down to NIT Consolation 2L, and every one was checked against the league's own bracket pages. 2003 stays blank forever — that was the Yahoo year, and MFL never had the games.

Eighteen years of AFL playoffs came back from the dead. Pick any season before 2024 and the brackets page said "Bracket data not available" — for the championship, for the NIT, for all of it. Turns out the games were never missing. MFL's bracket export only ever handed us seed numbers for those years, but the schedule had every playoff week sitting right there, fully scored, the whole time. The page now walks those weeks back into a bracket, so 2005 through 2023 finally show real matchups with real teams and real point totals: Cougs over Smokane, Chatmaster over the Limp Ditkas, No Frills over More Cowbell. One season stays blank: 2003, the year the league played on Yahoo, so MFL never had the games at all.

The consolation brackets are back too, which is the half of the postseason that actually decided things. The AFL Losers Bracket, the 3rd and 5th and 7th place games, and that magnificent tower of NIT losers brackets that handed out draft picks — all of it was blank for every season before 2024, and all of it is now filled in from the schedule. Worth knowing while you browse: MFL's own results page lies about finishing order for these years. The league wrote custom titles into its brackets, MFL read those titles as placements, and so it lists Da Dangsters second in 2005 when they actually finished third — they won the Losers Bracket. Second place was Smokane, who lost the title game to the Cougs. The brackets now on the page are built from games, not titles, so they show what actually happened.

The NIT tab was empty for fifteen seasons, and the reason is deeply stupid. The page decided which brackets were the championship and which were the NIT by their ID number — brackets 1 through 5 were the big dance, 6 through 9 were the NIT. That's true from 2018 on. It is not true for 2005 (NIT is bracket 3), or 2006 (bracket 4), or anything from 2007 to 2017 (bracket 5). So for fifteen years the NIT was quietly filed under Championship while the NIT tab sat there with nothing in it. The page now goes by the bracket's actual name, which has said "NIT" on it since 2003. The NIT Champion payout shows up for those seasons too, and the AFL Cup — an in-season thing from the 2012-2016 era that MFL never exported a single game for — stopped padding the page with seven empty cards.

The AFL playoff bracket was seeding old seasons with today's map. Pull up 2005 and the page sorted everyone into the four divisions the league runs now — except 2005 had six, three per conference, with a Central and a Pacific that haven't existed in over a decade. Twelve conference races between 2003 and 2016 came out seeded differently on the playoffs page than on the standings page for that very same season, which is a neat trick for a site to pull on itself. The playoffs page now reads each season's real structure, the same way standings already did.

Archived standings were showing the wrong divisions. Pull up 2015 and the site would group teams the way the league is organized TODAY — which is not how it was organized in 2015, or 2011, or 2008. Go back far enough and it got surreal: the 2007 season really had a Pacific, a Midwest and an Atlantic division, and the standings page was cheerfully sorting those teams into a Northwest and a Southwest that wouldn't exist for years. Twenty-one division races between 2007 and 2015 were showing a different winner than that team's own franchise page was — including the 2015 Central, the exact race we'd just spent a week proving belonged to the Amish Rakefighters. Every season now gets grouped the way it was actually played, straight from the league's own records, so the two finally tell the same story.

Settled a tiebreaker argument nobody knew we were having. Both rulebooks list 'Most Points Allowed' near the bottom of the standings tiebreakers — the idea being that if you're dead even with someone and you had to survive a tougher schedule of beatings, that should work in your favor. The code read it backwards and quietly rewarded the team that gave up FEWER points. Now a team that allowed more points wins that step, which means both the better spot in the standings and the earlier draft pick. Fair warning: this has never actually decided anything. In 76 seasons of TheLeague divisions and 106 of the AFL's, no tie has ever made it that far down the list. It's fixed for the day one finally does.

The Free Agents page finally noticed the rookie draft happened. The 'Include rookies' filter stayed off year-round, so every undrafted rookie — guys who are legitimately sitting in the player pool right now — was invisible unless you flipped the checkbox yourself. The page now reads the draft results: before and during the rookie draft the class stays tucked away like always, and once the final pick is in the books, the leftovers show up by default. Clearing filters respects whichever default the calendar says.

The AFL Franchises page traded its generic trophy/crown/shield/medal emoji for the league's actual championship badge art — the same medallions and shields from each team's trophy wall, stripped of their win-year so they read as lifetime totals. Premier League and D-League get their own small tier logos instead of banners that looked too much like the AFL championship medallion to tell apart at a glance.

The Show's franchise page finally let go of the grudge. The 2025 last-place punishment renamed them Cock Gobbler for a year, and even after the name reverted, the old nicknames lingered on the page as a public "aka Gobbler, Gobblers, Cock Gobbler" line — and showed up in assets-page search besides. The punitive year still lives on in the franchise's history archive where it belongs; the live page just doesn't advertise it anymore.

Search on TheLeague's site was pulling AFL-only pages into its results — type "keeper" looking for a rules question and you'd land on the AFL's Keeper Planner instead, a page that doesn't even apply to TheLeague's roster rules. The site directory is shared infrastructure across both leagues; TheLeague's search now only shows TheLeague's own pages.

The homepage's "Explore" quick-links grid had the same cross-league leak as search — three of its eight tiles were quietly pointing at AFL pages (Rosters, Standings, Free Agents) instead of TheLeague's own, and clicking any of them dead-ended in a 404. The grid now only pulls from TheLeague's own page list.

Managing a player in dark mode was a flashbang. Tap the three dots next to anyone on your AFL roster and the action menu came up as a stark white card — and worse, the player's name came up white ON that white card, so the one thing you needed to read was the one thing you couldn't. The card, the four action rows, the confirmation copy and the success and error banners now all wear the same navy the rest of the site does, with the AFL red showing up on hover where it belongs. Light mode looks exactly like it did yesterday.

In dark mode, the Premier League link in the sidebar menu was a crest you couldn't see. The badge is navy, the dark menu is navy, and the two met in the middle — leaving a label with a smudge where its logo should be. The rest of the site has had a dark version of that crest for a while, ringed with a halo so it reads against a dark background; the menu was the one place still loading the light-mode file off an old external address. It now uses the same artwork everything else does, D-League included, and it's served from our own site rather than fetched from elsewhere. Light mode is unchanged, except the crest no longer gets squashed into a square.

Your team card on the AFL homepage stopped spelling out your tier and conference and started showing them. Where the card used to print the word "Premier" under a stock trophy, it now leads with the actual Premier League crest — or the D-League one, if that's where the season left you — and the conference tile leads with the AL or NL mark instead of the letters and a generic star. Same badges the standings page has been using all along. While fitting them, it turned out the dark-mode versions of all four badges have been drawing about a tenth smaller than their light counterparts everywhere they appear — standings, the franchise cards, the playoff header — because of extra empty space baked into the artwork files. That's corrected, so the crests sit at their proper weight across the site. One knock-on: the countdown banners use the dark badge on their navy panel no matter which mode you're in, so their crest is a touch larger now in daylight too.
